title: Terminal
plain: A terminal is a program with a text window where you type commands and read the answers. It runs a shell, the program that understands your commands.
check: A terminal shows a line that ends in a symbol such as > or $, with a blinking cursor after it. What is the computer waiting for, and what happens when you press Enter?
rubric: Opens a terminal themselves, from the system or from the editor's Terminal menu
Types a command and presses Enter to run it
Tells the line they typed apart from the reply the computer printed
try: Open a terminal: on Windows search for Terminal or PowerShell, on macOS press Cmd+Space and type Terminal, on Linux look for Terminal in the app menu, or in VS Code use the menu Terminal, then New Terminal. Type `echo hello` and press Enter. The next line prints hello and then a new prompt appears.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the terminal is dangerous, and one wrong key can break the computer. Correct idea: it only runs what you type; commands that only show information (such as pwd and ls) change nothing, and an unknown command prints an error and nothing else.

title: Shell
plain: A shell is the program inside a terminal that reads your commands and runs them. Examples: bash and zsh on macOS and Linux, bash in Git Bash on Windows, and PowerShell on Windows.
check: A tutorial tells you to run `export NAME=Ada`, but your window shows the prompt `PS C:\projects\shop>` and prints a red error. Why did the command fail, and what is the first thing to check?
rubric: Names the shell from the prompt: PS C:\... means PowerShell, a prompt ending in $ or % usually means bash or zsh
Predicts that the command works in bash, zsh and Git Bash but fails in Windows PowerShell
Says that PowerShell needs different commands for the same jobs, for example ls -Force and $env:NAME = 'Ada'
try: Look at your prompt. In macOS, Linux or Git Bash run `echo $SHELL`: it prints your default shell, for example /bin/zsh or /usr/bin/bash. In PowerShell run `$PSVersionTable.PSVersion`: it prints a small table with the PowerShell version.
pitfall: Wrong belief: every terminal understands the same commands, so a pasted command always works. Correct idea: bash, zsh and PowerShell are different command languages, so check which shell a command was written for; on Windows, Codex runs commands in PowerShell.

title: Current folder, list files
plain: The current folder (working directory) is the folder the terminal is working in. `pwd` prints its path and `ls` lists what is inside it; in PowerShell, `dir` and `Get-ChildItem` also list it.
check: Two terminal windows are open on the same computer, and `ls` prints a different list in each. What is the most likely reason, and which command proves it?
rubric: Runs pwd (or Get-Location) and reads the printed path aloud
Runs ls (or dir) and points to one file and one folder in the output
Says that ls shows only the current folder, not the folders inside it
try: Open a terminal in your project folder. Run `pwd`: it prints the full path of the current folder (Git Bash writes it as /c/... for the C: drive). Run `ls`: it prints the names of the files and folders inside. Both commands also work in PowerShell, where they are aliases of Get-Location and Get-ChildItem.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a command works on the whole project, wherever the terminal is. Correct idea: the terminal always has one current folder, and a relative file name is looked up there, so run `pwd` before commands that create or change files.

title: Change folder (cd)
plain: `cd` (change directory) moves the terminal into another folder. `cd docs` goes into the docs folder inside the current folder, and `cd ..` goes up to the parent folder.
check: The prompt shows that you are in the folder `shop/src`. You run `cd ..` and then `cd docs`. Which folder are you in now, and what did each command change?
rubric: Writes down the expected folder before pressing Enter
Runs pwd after each cd and compares it with the prediction
Returns to the starting folder with cd .. or a path
try: In your project folder run `pwd`, then `cd ..` and `pwd` again: the second path is one folder shorter. Go back with `cd` and the project folder's name (for example `cd shop`), then run `pwd` once more to confirm you are where you started.
pitfall: Wrong belief: cd opens a folder or changes what is inside it. Correct idea: cd only changes which folder this terminal window works in; no file changes, and other terminal windows keep their own current folder.

title: Absolute and relative paths
plain: A path names where a file or folder is. An absolute path starts at the top (/projects/shop or C:\projects\shop); a relative path starts at the current folder (docs/notes.txt).
check: `python scripts/run.py` works in your project folder, but from your Desktop it prints `No such file or directory`. What is different, and how could you make the command work from both places?
rubric: Writes an absolute path that starts at the top (a drive letter or /)
Writes a relative path from the current folder, using .. when needed
Explains that a relative path depends on where the terminal currently is
try: Run `pwd` and `ls`, pick a folder name from the list and run `ls name` (a relative path). Run `ls .` (the current folder) and `ls ..` (the parent folder) and compare the lists. Run `ls ~` to list your home folder; `~` means the home folder in bash, zsh, Git Bash and PowerShell.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a path is the same as a file name and works from any folder. Correct idea: a relative path is read from the current folder, so the same text can point to another file, or to nothing, when you are somewhere else; Windows paths use backslashes and a drive letter, while macOS and Linux paths use forward slashes.

title: Command, arguments, flags
plain: A command line is a program name plus arguments (what to work on) and options or flags (how to work): git commit -m "fix typo". Spaces separate parts; quotes keep words together.
check: In `cp "my notes.txt" backup/`, which words are the arguments, and what would the shell do with the command if you removed the quotes?
rubric: Names the program, the flag and the arguments in a command such as cp "my notes.txt" backup/
Explains that the shell splits the line at spaces unless quotes group the words
Predicts the error that appears when the quotes are removed
try: In a scratch folder (not inside a project) run `mkdir "my notes"`, then `ls`: you see a folder named my notes. Run `cd my notes` without quotes: you get an error (the wording depends on the shell). Run `cd "my notes"` with quotes: it works. Leave with `cd ..` and remove the empty folder with `rmdir "my notes"`.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the terminal guesses what you mean, so extra spaces or missing quotes do not matter. Correct idea: the shell splits the line at spaces and runs exactly those words, so one wrong character gives an error or a different command.

title: Reading --help
signals: how do i use this command
plain: Most commands can print a help text. Add `--help` after the command, or run `man command` (macOS, Linux) or `Get-Help command` (PowerShell), to see what it does, its options and their order.
check: A help text starts with `usage: git status [<options>] [--] [<pathspec>...]`. What do the square brackets and the angle brackets tell you about what to type?
rubric: Shows the help text with --help, or with man or Get-Help for their shell
Reads the usage line: square brackets mark optional parts and angle brackets mark a value to replace with their own
Runs the command with one option and compares the output with their prediction
try: Run `git --help`: it prints a usage line and a list of common Git commands. Run `git status -h`: it prints a short usage line and the options of that one command. Pick one option, for example -s, and run `git status -s` in a folder that is a Git project to see what it does. Note that `git status --help` opens the full manual page in a browser or a pager instead; press `q` to leave a pager.
pitfall: Wrong belief: developers memorize every command and flag. Correct idea: they look options up all the time with --help, man pages or the documentation, so reading a usage line is the skill to practice.

title: Stopping a program (Ctrl+C)
plain: A process is a running program. A program that keeps running, like a local web server, holds the prompt until you stop it. Press Ctrl+C in its window to ask it to quit.
check: A server is running in your terminal and you want to run `git status` without stopping it. What are two ways to do that?
rubric: Starts the program and sees that the prompt does not come back
Presses Ctrl+C in the window where the program runs, not in another window
Sees the prompt return, and says how to run another command while the program runs (a second terminal tab)
try: In an empty scratch folder run `python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` (python3 on macOS and Linux). It prints that it is serving on port 8000 and the prompt does not come back. Open http://localhost:8000 in a browser to see a directory listing. Click the terminal window and press Ctrl+C: Python prints `Keyboard interrupt received, exiting.` and the prompt returns.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Ctrl+C copies text, as in most programs. Correct idea: in a terminal it asks the running program to stop (copy is Cmd+C on macOS, usually Ctrl+Shift+C on Linux, and Ctrl+C or Ctrl+Shift+C in Windows Terminal when text is selected); inside Codex, Esc interrupts a running task, and Ctrl+C or /exit closes the Codex CLI.

title: Copy, move, delete files
plain: mkdir makes a folder, cp copies, mv moves or renames, and rm deletes. Deleting in the terminal skips the trash or recycle bin, so a deleted file cannot be restored from there.
check: A command `rm -r build` is waiting at your prompt. What do you want to know before pressing Enter, and which commands tell you?
rubric: Runs ls before rm and names the exact target
Deletes one named file, not a wildcard or a whole folder, for the first delete
Says that the deleted file is not in the trash and cannot be undone from the terminal
try: In a scratch folder run, one line at a time: `mkdir practice`, `cd practice`, `echo hello > a.txt`, `cp a.txt b.txt`, `mv b.txt c.txt`, `ls` (you see a.txt and c.txt), `rm c.txt`, `ls` (only a.txt remains). Clean up with `rm a.txt`, `cd ..` and `rmdir practice`, which removes only an empty folder. These commands work in bash, zsh and PowerShell; only the look of the ls output differs.
pitfall: Wrong belief: rm works like the Delete key, so the file can be restored from the trash. Correct idea: rm and PowerShell's Remove-Item delete at once and skip the trash, usually without a question; in bash and zsh, cp and mv also replace a file of the same name without asking.

title: Environment variables
plain: An environment variable is a named value, such as HOME or PATH, that a program receives from the process that starts it. Programs read them for settings and secrets instead of keeping those in code.
check: You set a variable in one terminal window and cannot see it in a second window. Why, and where could you store it so that every new window has it?
rubric: Sets the variable with the syntax of their shell (export NAME=value or $env:NAME = 'value') and shows with a one-line Python command that a program started from that window can read it
Predicts that a new terminal window does not have the variable
Names a place for a permanent value: a shell startup file, the system's environment-variable settings, or a project .env file that the program reads
try: Print an existing one: `echo $HOME` (macOS, Linux, Git Bash) or `$env:USERPROFILE` (PowerShell). Set one for this window only: `export GREETING=hi` (bash, zsh, Git Bash) or `$env:GREETING = 'hi'` (PowerShell). Read it from a program: `python -c "import os; print(os.environ.get('GREETING'))"` (python3 on macOS and Linux) prints hi. Open a second window and run the Python line again: it prints None.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a variable I set stays set everywhere and for good. Correct idea: it lives only in that window and in programs started from it, and a new window starts without it.

title: PATH, command not found
plain: PATH is an environment variable that lists folders. When you type a command name, the shell searches those folders, in order, for a program with that name. If none matches, it prints 'command not found'.
check: You install a tool and the installer says it worked, yet typing the tool's name prints 'command not found'. What are two possible causes, and which command would you use to test each?
rubric: Checks the spelling of the command first
Opens a new terminal window, because PATH is read when a window starts
Looks where the tool lives with which, where.exe or Get-Command, and checks that this folder is in PATH
try: Type a command that does not exist, `nosuchcommand`, and read the error: bash says 'command not found', zsh says 'command not found: nosuchcommand', PowerShell says the term 'is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet'. Then find a real program: `which git` (macOS, Linux, Git Bash) or `Get-Command git` or `where.exe git` (PowerShell; plain `where` is a different command there). It prints the full path that PATH found.
pitfall: Wrong belief: 'command not found' means the program is not installed. Correct idea: it may be installed while its folder is not in PATH, or this window started before the install and still has the old PATH; open a new terminal and check with which, where.exe or Get-Command.

title: Exit codes
plain: When a program ends it returns an exit code, a number. 0 means success; any other number means failure. Shells, scripts and tools read this number to decide what to do next.
check: In bash or zsh, `ls nosuchfile` fails. You type `echo $?` and then type `echo $?` a second time. What does each one print, and why do they differ?
rubric: Predicts 0 for success and a non-zero number for failure
Reads the code right after the command (echo $? in bash and zsh, $LASTEXITCODE in PowerShell, echo %ERRORLEVEL% in CMD)
Says that the next command replaces the stored code
try: Run `python -c "import sys; sys.exit(3)"` (python3 on macOS and Linux), then show its exit code: `echo $?` in bash, zsh and Git Bash, `$LASTEXITCODE` in PowerShell, `echo %ERRORLEVEL%` in CMD. It prints 3. Run `python -c "print('ok')"` and show the code again: it prints 0.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if no error text appeared, the command succeeded. Correct idea: the exit code is the official result; a program can print a warning and still return 0, or print nothing and return 1.

title: Pipes and redirection
plain: A pipe (`|`) sends one command's output into another command as input. Redirection sends output into a file instead: `>` replaces the file's content and `>>` adds to the end.
check: You run `echo first > notes.txt` and then `echo second > notes.txt`. What does notes.txt contain, and which one-character change would keep both lines?
rubric: Predicts that nothing is printed on screen because the output went into the file
Predicts that > replaces the old content and >> adds a line at the end
Shows the file content with cat to check the prediction
try: In a scratch folder run `echo banana > fruit.txt`, then `echo apple >> fruit.txt`, then `cat fruit.txt`: it shows banana and apple. Now run `cat fruit.txt | sort`: the same lines appear sorted, apple first. The commands work in bash, zsh and PowerShell.
pitfall: Wrong belief: > only shows or copies output and is harmless. Correct idea: > replaces the target file at once without asking, so check the file name first and use >> when you want to add to the end.

title: sudo and administrator
plain: Some actions need administrator rights. On macOS and Linux, `sudo` runs one command as the administrator (root); on Windows you choose Run as administrator. Commands with these rights can change or delete anything.
check: A tutorial says `sudo npm install -g some-tool` fixes your 'EACCES permission denied' error. What would you give up by running it, and what would you ask first?
rubric: Reads the whole error to find which file or folder was refused
Asks whether the command should touch that place at all
Names a safer fix before sudo, such as running in the right folder, fixing the folder's owner or installing into the user's own folder
try: Run `whoami`: it prints the account your terminal uses. Then read a protected place and look at the refusal: Linux `ls /root`, macOS `ls /private/var/root`, Windows PowerShell `ls C:\Windows\System32\config`. You see an error such as Permission denied, or in PowerShell Access to the path is denied. Do not use sudo to get past it. Windows 11 version 24H2 or newer also has an optional sudo command that you turn on in Settings, under System and Advanced.
pitfall: Wrong belief: when a command says 'permission denied', adding sudo is the normal fix. Correct idea: the refusal protects the system and sudo gives the command full power, so first find out which place is protected and why; never run sudo on a command you do not understand.

title: Package managers
plain: A package manager downloads and installs software from an online catalog with one command. winget (Windows), Homebrew (macOS) and apt (Debian, Ubuntu) install programs; npm (JavaScript) and pip (Python) install code libraries for projects.
check: Both `winget install git` and `pip install requests` install something. What is different about what they install and where it ends up?
rubric: Says that winget installs a program for the whole computer, while pip installs a Python library into the active Python environment
Names where each ends up: winget in the system's program folders, pip in the Python installation or in a virtual environment folder
Checks the exact spelling of the name and who publishes the package before installing it
try: Check which managers you have, without installing anything: `pip --version` (pip3 on some systems), `npm --version`, and on Windows `winget --version`, on macOS `brew --version`, on Debian or Ubuntu `apt --version`. Each prints a version, or an error such as command not found if it is missing. Then list what is installed: `pip list` or `npm list --depth=0`.
pitfall: Wrong belief: installing from a package manager is always safe because it is official. Correct idea: an install downloads code from the internet and can run it, and attackers publish packages with look-alike names, so type names carefully and ask what a package is before installing it.

title: Install Git and Python
plain: Git records saved versions of your project, and Python runs the scripts you write. Install each from its official download page, then check it with a version command.
check: Your terminal says that python is not recognized right after you installed Python. What is the most likely cause, and which command shows whether Python works now?
rubric: Names the likely cause: Python is not installed, or the terminal was open before the install and does not know the new program yet
Runs python --version (python3 --version on macOS and Linux) and reads the version line, or the message that the program is missing
Says to open a new terminal first, and to install from the official download page if the command still fails
try: Open a terminal and run git --version, then python --version (on macOS and Linux run python3 --version). Each prints one line with the program name and a version number. If you see 'not recognized' (Windows) or 'command not found' (macOS and Linux), the program is not installed yet: install it from https://git-scm.com/install/ for Git or https://www.python.org/downloads/ for Python, then close the terminal, open a new one and run the command again.
pitfall: Wrong belief: once the installer has finished, every open terminal can run the new program. Correct idea: a terminal reads its list of known programs only when it starts, so close it and open a new one before you judge the install.
